title: The universe in his mouth
hookLine: Yashoda looks in her toddler's mouth for dirt and sees the whole universe, herself included
carry: the little one holds the whole universe

cards: Mother, Krishna ate dirt! The other boys come running to tell on him, his older brother Balarama among them. He has just put a handful of earth in his mouth.
Yashoda grabs him by the hand, scolds him, and asks why. And the little boy, dirt on his lips, looks his mother in the eye and denies everything.

teach.b: I didn't eat any dirt, Mother. They're lying. If you think they're telling the truth, look in my mouth yourself.
So he opens it, and she looks in. And there, inside her son's mouth, she sees everything.
The Bhagavata lists it all: the sky and the directions, the mountains, the islands and oceans, the whole round earth, wind and fire, the moon and the stars. The turning of time. The gods.
The elements that make up a body, and the mind itself.

teach.h: THE VILLAGE, AND HERSELF IN IT.
teach.b: And in among all of it, the village of Vraja, and in the village, herself. She's standing in her yard looking into her son's mouth, and inside it she finds her yard, and herself standing in it. She's frightened.
Is this a dream? Is this an illusion sent by God? Is my own mind confused?
Or is it some power that belongs to my child? So she bows, inwardly, to the one beyond all thought, in whom all of this rests. Here's the teaching, and it's one of Hinduism's biggest.
The God Hindus love as a little boy is not a small god.
The baby she nurses, the one who steals the neighbors' butter, holds everything that is, her included.
Teachers often set this beside the Bhagavad Gita, where Arjuna sees the whole universe inside Krishna on a battlefield, and trembles. Yashoda sees it in her own yard.

That's why a Hindu family can keep a tiny brass baby Krishna on the shrine, feed him and rock him, and still pray to him as Lord of everything. The small form doesn't make God small. It makes God close enough to hold.

how: Krishna devotees tell this story alongside the butter-thief stories, and devotional paintings and songs show Yashoda peering into the child's open mouth.

practice: Yesterday you met darshan: seeing God, and being seen. Try it again. Look at an image of Krishna, or any sacred image, for a few breaths.
Then let it open, as Yashoda's vision did: sky, oceans, stars, your street, and you, all held inside that small form. Come back to the image, and bow if you like.
If you don't pray, look at a photo of a small child you love, and remember how much is inside them.
